title: In the beginning there was nothing; death covered it (1.2)
hook: a second creation story, stranger than Uddalaka's: at first there was nothing here at all, covered by death, which is hunger
tomorrow: the gods and demons and the breath

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashvamedha, the opening of the Brihadaranyaka. Your line was the dawn is its head. Did you catch the first light? Day three hundred sixty-one.

Twenty days ago, Uddalaka told his son: in the beginning there was Being alone, and it thought, let me be many. Calm, almost serene. Now open the Brihadaranyaka to its second section, and you get a very different first sentence. In the beginning there was nothing here at all. All this was covered by death. And death, it says, is hunger. Two great Upanishads, two creation stories. Hindu tradition has kept them both, side by side.
screen: `BEING ALONE, CALM AND SERENE.` → `NOW: NOTHING, COVERED BY DEATH.` → `TWO STORIES, KEPT SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit it begins: naiveha kimcanagra asit. Nothing at all was here in the beginning. Mrityunaivedam avritam asit, ashanayaya. This was covered by death, by hunger. Ashanaya hi mrityuh: for hunger is death. Then death does something. It makes a mind, thinking: let me have a self. It moves about, chanting praise, and from its praise water arises. The froth on the water hardens into the earth. Death toils, and from its heat, fire is born. Then it wants a second self, and through the mind, it joins with speech. The seed becomes the year. Before that, the text says, there was no year. When the year is born, death opens its mouth to swallow it, and the newborn cries out, bhan! That cry becomes speech. Death thinks: if I eat this, I'll have less food. So instead, through speech, it brings forth everything: the verses of the Vedas, the rituals, people, animals. And whatever it brings forth, it begins to eat. Then death longs to offer a greater sacrifice. It toils, and its body swells, and the text plays on a word: the swollen one, ashva, the horse. There's yesterday's horse, back again. What does it mean that the world comes from hunger? One way to hear it: everything alive wants. Eats, reaches, grows, consumes. The text looks straight at that and says it goes all the way down, to the first stirring of anything at all. Hunger isn't an accident in the world. In this story, it's where the world came from.
screen: `NOTHING HERE, COVERED BY DEATH.` · `FOR HUNGER IS DEATH.` · `THE NEWBORN YEAR CRIES OUT: BHAN!` · `THE SWOLLEN ONE: THE HORSE.` · then, large: `FROM HUNGER, THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice watches hunger without obeying it. Sit and settle. Notice any wanting in you right now: for food, for your phone, for the sit to end, for something to happen. Don't act on it. Don't push it away. Just watch it, the way you'd watch weather. Notice how it rises, leans forward, and sometimes fades on its own. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Ashanaya, hunger. The Brihadaranyaka's creation: nothing, covered by death, which is hunger, and from that hunger, mind, water, earth, fire, speech and the world.
Your line: from hunger, the world. Today, notice one want as it rises, and let it pass once without feeding it. Day three hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Hindu scriptures contain many creation accounts, from the Rig Veda's hymns to the Upanishads and Puranas, and teachers generally present them side by side as different windows rather than as a single official version.

match.prompt: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

myth: this story begins with Being alone, one without a second
that's the Chandogya. the Brihadaranyaka begins with nothing, covered by death.
the text says hunger is death
the newborn year's cry becomes speech
death opens its mouth to swallow it, and it cries out: bhan!

fork.setup: you're death, in this story. you've just brought forth the year, and you open your mouth to eat it. it cries out. what do you do?
options: think: if I eat this, I'll have less food, and bring forth everything else instead.
give up and go back to nothing.
fork.reveal: death spares it, and through speech brings forth the Vedas, rituals, people and animals, and then begins to eat all it made.

original.note: Sanskrit aśanāyā: hunger, the wish to eat. aśanāyā hi mṛtyuḥ: for hunger is death.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy creation myth.
what it means: the drive to want and consume is treated as the root of the world itself: from hunger, the world.
what a scholar hears: Brihadaranyaka 1.2, full of wordplay (arka from arc and ka; ashva from ashvat, swelled), and it explains the horse sacrifice of 1.1.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.2.1–7 (death, hunger; mind; water, earth, fire; the year; bhan; ashva)

notes: Sanskrit of 1.2.1 in simplified transliteration (naiveha kiṃcanāgra āsīn mṛtyunaivedam āvṛtam āsīd aśanāyayā, aśanāyā hi mṛtyuḥ); only the first phrase is listed as quoted, the rest appears in the voice from the same verse. Confirm.

Story details paraphrased: water from death's worship (arka wordplay), froth becoming earth, fire from its toil, union of mind and speech producing the year, the cry 'bhan' becoming speech (1.2.4), aditi from 'ad' (omitted), ashva from 'ashvat' (1.2.7). Confirm each.

Hook now says 'twenty days ago' (day 341), corrected from 'three weeks ago'. Also softened 'Hindu tradition keeps them both ... without forcing them to agree' to 'has kept them both, side by side', since Vedanta commentators do work to harmonize the creation accounts.
howItsDone generalizes that teachers 'generally' present creation accounts side by side; confirm this is fair across traditions.
